pending_articles.title: Sensitivity at the Edges of the Finger Enables Mixed Reality Force Feedback
pending_articles.content: We introduce a new paradigm for rendering high-force sensations by stimulating the edges of the fingerpad rather than the central contact surface. This non-blocking approach preserves natural finger use, enabling simultaneous physical and virtual interactions. To investigate its feasibility, we proposed a mechanotransduction mechanism and conducted biomechanical and psychophysical studies. Our results show that the fingerpad edges are nearly as sensitive as the center under low forces, become roughly 117% more sensitive under moderate forces, and maintain sensitivity at higher forces. The edges also exhibit increased stiffness and tolerate higher forces before discomfort. Furthermore, the left edge exhibited approximately 143% higher sensitivity than the right edge in the right hand. Using these insights, we built a compact wearable device that provides multi-DOF force feedback without blocking the fingerpad and demonstrated its use in VR/AR scenarios. These findings support edge-based stimulation as a viable approach for high-force, scalable haptic feedback in mixed reality and teleoperation systems.

pending_articles.title: ThermalTexture: Temperature-Integrated Surface Rendering Using Thermal Referral Induced by Texture Slip-Feedback
pending_articles.content: Thermal–vibration feedback has been reported to elicit the thermal referral phenomenon, offering new possibilities for enhancing user experience. Yet, little research has explored whether thermal referral occurs in the presence of texture-slip feedback. To address this, we developed a custom haptic device capable of delivering integrated thermal and slip feedback to the middle and distal phalanges of an index finger. We primarily estimated the thermal referral occurrence under passive and active touch conditions across two different perceptual experiments, while each further examined its impact on texture perceptions and user experiences (UX). In Perceptual Experiment 1 (passive), we observed the highest occurrence of thermal referral at 40 $^{\circ }\mathrm{C}$ (0.86 on a 0–1 scale), and found that referral increased the median of perceived roughness from 43.5 to 60 on a 0—100 scale. In Perceptual Experiment 2 (active), the kinesthetic cues significantly enhanced thermal referral, with the occurrence probability at 24 $^{\circ }\mathrm{C}$ increasing to 0.86 compared to 0.51 (0—1 scale) in the first study. In addition, high UX ratings demonstrated the applicability of our device to temperature-integrated virtual texture interactions. Our findings expand the scope of thermal referral and highlight the potential for enabling VR users to interact with virtual surfaces that provide temperature cues.

pending_articles.title: Beyond Mean Pooling: Statistical Meta-Aggregation for Subject-Level EEG Classification in Parkinson's Disease
pending_articles.content: Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a non-invasive, temporally precise tool for studying neural alterations associated with Parkinson's disease (PD). When labels are defined at the subject level but inputs are epoch level, a key design choice is how epoch-wise predictions are aggregated to a single subject-level decision. Most prior work uses mean pooling, which assumes all epochs contribute equally and independently. This study proposes a statistical meta-aggregation strategy that represents each subject by 14 descriptors of the epoch-wise prediction distribution, including measures of central tendency, dispersion, shape, and high-confidence concentration. Using a self-supervised contrastive encoder trained on task-evoked EEG from the Simon conflict task, and a sample of 90 subjects including 57 PD and 33 control, this work evaluates the proposed framework under subject-wise five-fold cross-validation. Replacing mean pooling with statistical meta-aggregation lifts subject-level ROC-AUC from 0.655 to 0.872 for logistic regression and from 0.724 to 0.840 for support vector machines, without modifying the encoder or the classifier family. Averaging predictions across three independent self-supervised pretraining seeds yields competitive performance and improved balanced accuracy. These results suggest that, in this dataset, the way epoch-level predictions are summarized at the subject level has a substantial effect on final PD classification performance.

pending_articles.title: Optimising neural contrast and minimising tissue shrinkage in dragon lizard brains: buffered Lugol's iodine versus phosphotungstic acid for contrast-enhanced μCT
pending_articles.content: Contrast-enhanced micro-computed tomography (CT) has become a valuable tool for addressing neuroanatomical questions that previously required destructive histology. As a relatively new technique, it remains subject to ongoing technical refinement, and taxon- and tissue-specific protocol optimisation. We evaluated the performance of two common contrast-enhancing agents, buffered Lugol's iodine and phosphotungstic acid (PTA) in aqueous solution, for CT visualisation of the nervous system in the Jacky dragon lizard, Amphibolurus muricatus by comparing staining time, contrast specificity and brain tissue shrinkage evaluated at three concentrations (1.25%, 2.5% and 5%). Buffered Lugol's iodine outperformed aqueous PTA by requiring shorter staining times (as short as four days) and providing better white matter-grey matter differentiation, whereas PTA required longer incubation periods of approximately three weeks and produced poorer white-grey matter differentiation. Importantly, buffered Lugol's iodine produced higher brain-to-endocast occupancy estimates than aqueous PTA, suggesting substantially reduced tissue shrinkage. PTA-treated specimens exhibited an estimated 13.3% reduction in occupancy and approximately 20% greater brain tissue shrinkage than buffered Lugol's-treated specimens. Together, these findings demonstrate that buffered Lugol's iodine staining provides the high level of internal tissue contrast required to resolve fine-scale neuroanatomical organisation in three dimensions, preserves the spatial relationships among anatomical structures, and reduces artefacts, all of which result in a closer correspondence between the brain and endocranial cavity. From a practical perspective, the study provides guidance for contrast agent selection in future CT studies and reveals that buffered Lugol's iodine is better suited to fine-scale neuroanatomical, volumetric and geometric morphometric analyses, whereas PTA is advantageous for applications prioritising general soft-tissue or musculoskeletal visualisation.

pending_articles.title: Enhancing cortical electrophysiological signatures of sleep overrides ER stress responses in sleep-deprived mice
pending_articles.content: Sleep deprivation (SD) triggers characteristic changes in the cortical electroencephalogram (EEG) during waking and sleep, as well as upregulating molecular signatures of neuronal activity, synaptic plasticity, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress. This includes the induction of the unfolded protein response (UPR), the primary marker and adaptive mechanism of ER stress. Yet how cortical neuronal activity during SD contributes to the induction of these molecular signatures remains unknown. Here we investigate whether manipulating cortical activity during SD with a physiological stimulation paradigm (flickering light stimulation, FLS) affects the induction of the UPR. As expected, SD alone upregulated activity-dependent and UPR-related genes in cortex and led to increased EEG slow-wave activity (SWA) during subsequent NREM sleep, an electrophysiological signature of sleep need. Delivering FLS during SD, however, prevented the upregulation of activity- and UPR-related genes while inducing an additional increase in SWA during subsequent sleep. Further analysis of neuronal firing revealed that FLS induced brief neuronal silent (OFF) periods in awake animals during stimulation, thereby shifting cortical activity towards a brain state resembling sleep. These findings suggest that physiological manipulation of cortical activity during waking is sufficient to dissociate molecular signatures of ER stress from electrophysiological markers of sleep pressure. We propose that global sleep wake history and cortical network dynamics differentially regulate activity-dependent transcription and the accumulation of sleep pressure.

recently_processed.title: Active Lubrication Brakes in Tabletop and Hand-Held Haptic Surgical Drilling Simulators
recently_processed.content: Haptic user interfaces that provide both kinesthetic and vibrotactile feedback have strong potential to enhance a wide range of medical training simulations. Yet, designing such devices remains challenging due to constraints related to integration, workspace, cost, and the need for diverse feedback types. To address these issues, we investigated the applicability of a novel type of brake based on the active lubrication principle. This actuator is compact, low-cost, and able to deliver both kinesthetic and vibrotactile feedback. To demonstrate its advantages, we focused on maxillofacial drilling in surgical training. We designed, implemented and evaluated a one-degree-of-freedom drill mock-up embedded into a tabletop prototype able to render axial forces up to 4.5 N. To assess both the relevance of combined feedback and the suitability of this actuator for surgical simulation, we conducted two studies: one with fourteen non-surgeon participants and another with six maxillofacial surgeons. Results confirm the potential of this actuation approach for surgery simulators and highlighted the importance of combined kinesthetic and vibrotactile feedback to improve realism, user preference, and task performance. Based on the surgeons’ feedback, we then proposed a redesigned brake, with an improved control method, implemented in a new hand-held version of a drill replica. Preliminary characterisation shows that the new prototype can render forces up to 5.5 N and produce higher vibration amplitudes than the initial design.

recently_processed.title: Reconciling Reduced the Sense of Ownership and Agency Toward a Virtual Keypad With Enhanced Haptic Experience Using Visually Adjusted Self-Haptics for Key-Input Interaction
recently_processed.content: Self-Haptics is a tactile feedback technique where users utilize their own body to generate tactile sensations. This method allows the body to act purely as a prop, making it useful for virtual objects and user interfaces not directly related to the body. However, any method for maintaining the sense of ownership (SoO) and agency (SoA) of the user’s body and interaction targets that aligns with the perceptual interaction by visual cues has not been established. To address this, we present the concept of “(Not My) Self-Haptics,” which aims to resolve these inconsistencies, leveraging vision’s dominance in sensory integration. In this study, through the user’s interaction with a virtual keypad (VPad) displayed at the position of the real hand (RHand), we clarified how the user’s experience changed, including SoO and SoA toward the VPad, and how the task performance was affected by the interaction with the VPad. The results show that displaying the VHand at a misaligned position with the RHand or hiding the VHand significantly reduces SoO and SoA toward the VPad. Conversely, obtaining tactile feedback through Self-Haptics during interaction with the VPad significantly decreases task performance and increases SoO toward the VPad displayed near the VHand. Despite these unintended effects, this visual modification also significantly enhances Autotelics, Involvement, and Realism based on the Haptic Experience Inventory compared to typical mid-air interaction without tactile feedback. These findings contribute to the understanding of the interaction between visual and tactile sensations in Self-Haptics and the feasibility and practicality of “(Not My) Self-Haptics”.

recently_processed.title: VibGrasp: Spatiotemporal Vibration Based Multimodal Haptic Rendering With a Lightweight Exo-Glove for 3D Shape Perception
recently_processed.content: Haptic feedback has been employed to enhance shape perception during grasp interactions, improving immersion and task performance in extended reality (XR). Although wearable devices offer precise multi-phalangeal haptic feedback, their bulkiness and complexity often hinder practicality. In addition, fingertip-based tactile feedback often limits users’ ability to perceive a continuous and sequential sensation across the finger surfaces during power grasp. We present VibGrasp, a haptic shape-rendering method and a supporting haptic glove that synchronizes spatiotemporal vibrotactile feedback across multiple phalanges with 1-DOF kinesthetic feedback. Using the funneling illusion and duration-modulated vibration patterns, our approach delivers sequential, continuous sensations along the finger to render various shapes. We also develop a lightweight exoskeleton glove with two dorsal-mounted vibration actuators designed to transmit feedback to the ventral surfaces without obstructing motion. Two perception studies demonstrated consistent shape associations and clear preferences for specific patterns. A VR user-experience study further showed that VibGrasp achieved higher ratings for realism, satisfaction, and harmony than prior approaches. These findings offer insights into improving immersive and efficient haptic shape rendering in XR.

recently_processed.title: Propeller-Based Handheld Force-Feedback Device for Navigation
recently_processed.content: This article presents an evaluation of CrazyJoystick, a propeller-based handheld force-feedback device, for spatial navigation tasks in real-world and virtual reality environments. Building upon prior work validating the device's on-demand aerial deployment and directional cue discriminability, we investigated whether propeller-based kinesthetic torque cues can support effective wayfinding during continuous locomotion. We developed navigation-specific algorithms that generate egocentric directional cues using hierarchical decision logic optimized for dynamic heading corrections. Two user studies (N = 12) compared CrazyJoystick with vibrotactile baselines. Study 1 evaluated multi-waypoint navigation through four path configurations in a real-world environment with visual occlusion; CrazyJoystick reduced completion time by 54.6% and path deviation by 25.8% relative to vibrotactile guidance. Study 2 assessed target localization in a VR treasure hunt with minimal lighting; CrazyJoystick enabled 43.2% faster completion and 79% higher walking speeds. Both studies revealed consistent workload reductions. These findings demonstrate that propeller-based kinesthetic feedback supports efficient navigation during sustained locomotion, establishing propeller-based torque directional cues as a viable alternative to vibrotactile encoding for dynamic wayfinding tasks.

recently_processed.title: A Wearable Shoulder Skin-Deformation Device Generating Illusory Forces for Posture Correction
recently_processed.content: The hanger reflex is a haptic illusion in which skin-shear deformation elicits a directional force sensation. This study presents a wearable haptic device that uses four pneumatic airbags to apply controlled skin shear to both shoulders for posture guidance. Although previous work has shown that shoulder skin shear can induce illusory forces, neither the magnitude of these forces nor their influence on upper-body posture has been quantitatively examined. In Experiment 1, we quantified perceived force using a psychophysical comparison between skin-shear stimulation and real traction forces. The device generated perceived forces of up to 4.4 N in the forward direction and 4.8 N in the backward direction, more than an order of magnitude larger than those reported for conventional illusion-based haptic methods. Perceived force increased systematically with air pressure and was well approximated by a linear model. In Experiment 2, we evaluated the effects of these stimuli on upper-body posture by measuring trunk pitch under varying initial postures, stimulation directions, and intensities. The device induced consistent posture adjustments, particularly in the backward direction, with significant effects of both initial posture and stimulus intensity. These results demonstrate that shoulder hanger-reflex stimulation provides strong, controllable force sensations and measurable posture modification, supporting its use in wearable posture-support and rehabilitation systems.

recently_processed.title: Astrocytic sEH-EET signaling regulates microglial lysosomal function and suppresses the STING-Type I interferon pathway in Alzheimer's disease
recently_processed.content: Background: The development of {beta}-amyloid (A{beta}) pathology in Alzheimer's disease (AD) is accompanied by profound changes in astrocytes and microglia and associated neuroinflammation. Soluble epoxide hydrolase (sEH), which degrades anti-inflammatory epoxyeicosatrienoic acids (EETs), is elevated in the AD brain, yet how EETs restrain inflammation remains poorly understood. Methods: We performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) on brains from wild-type, sEH knockout, 5xFAD, and 5xFAD; sEH knockout mice, and used primary mouse microglia and human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived microglia to define the underlying mechanism. To test cell-type-specific contributions, we generated astrocyte- and endothelial-specific she knockout mice and crossed them with 5xFAD mice. Results: Genetic disruption of sEH in 5xFAD mice markedly reduced the abundance of a type I interferon (IFN)-responsive microglial subcluster and lowered phospho-STING (pSTING) levels. In primary microglia, supplementation with 11,12-EET attenuated STING activation and IFN target gene expression; blocking lysosomal acidification abolished this effect and caused pSTING to accumulate, identifying lysosomal degradation as a critical route for terminating STING signaling. 11,12-EET also enhanced microglial lysosomal acidification and A{beta} phagocytosis. Astrocytic, but not endothelial, disruption of sEH recapitulated the reductions in A{beta} pathology and microglial STING activation seen in global sEH-deficient mice, identifying astrocytes as the major cellular source of EETs regulating this pathway. Conclusion: We define an astrocyte-microglia axis in which astrocytic sEH limits EET availability and thereby sustains microglial STING signaling. By promoting lysosomal clearance of pSTING, EETs suppress type I IFN signaling and enhance microglial A{beta} clearance, highlighting sEH inhibition as a therapeutic strategy targeting both neuroinflammation and lysosomal dysfunction in AD.
recently_processed.author: Ghosh, B., Wang, S., Qi, C., Ghosh, A., Comerota, M., Rajpurohit, C. S., Zeldin, D. C., Zheng, H.

recently_processed.title: Comparing re-referencing methods for human intracranial EEG
recently_processed.content: Stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG) involves the implantation of depth electrodes in the brain to monitor epileptic seizures for surgical feasibility. As the electrodes advance into deeper limbic structures, the macro contacts distributed along the shaft record electrical activity from more lateral sites, while a bundled array of microwires simultaneously captures highly localised signals from the tip of the electrode. In a clinical setting these electrical signals are recorded relative to a reference signal, which may be sub-optimal for subsequent analyses that are unrelated to clinical objectives. Therefore, a secondary re-referencing operation is often undertaken to transform the signal in relation to a specific hypothesis. Despite a recent surge in SEEG studies, comparative studies on the much-understudied issue of re-referencing are sparse. Here, we analyse data collected from 16 human patients during an episodic memory task and comparatively apply a range of re-referencing methods to both macro contact and micro-wire data. We find that the choice of method changes the proportion of trials that survive artefact rejection, low frequency power, and the aperiodic background against which that power is read. In the hippocampal recordings, however, no method differed from any other in the size of a memory effect in power or spike-field coherence. This early transformative decision therefore bears on how the signal is described. We found no evidence that it changes the detectability of the behavioural effects tested here, and no method reversed the direction of a memory effect.

recently_processed.title: Learned Audiovisual Predictability Modulates Depth-Resolved Hippocampal-Cortical Functional Coupling
recently_processed.content: Perception reflects the dynamic integration of prior expectations, uncertainty, and incoming sensory evidence, but the neural circuitry supporting these computations remains debated. Current theories implicate coordinated interactions between the hippocampus and neocortex, potentially at the level of hippocampal subfields and cortical layers. Evidence in humans has come primarily from the visual domain, while less is known about how these interactions support learned auditory predictions. Using submillimetre 7T fMRI, we investigated depth-resolved functional coupling between hippocampal subfields and temporal and frontal cortical regions during audiovisual associative prediction. Participants learned deterministic associations between visual cues and auditory syllables, allowing us to compare auditory processing in predictable and unpredictable contexts. Predictability-related connectivity changes showed a spatially structured pattern involving DG/CA3-pSTG and CA1-inferior frontal regions, with significant edge-wise effects resolved across cortical depths. These findings provide fine-grained evidence that learned auditory predictability modulates hippocampal-cortical functional interactions across temporo-frontal systems.
recently_processed.author: Sozzi, S., Enan, M., Auksztulewicz, R., Schwiedrzik, C., Melloni, L., Esposito, F., Vanello, N., De Martino, F.

recently_processed.title: Intelligent systems distribute memory across internal and embodied resources
recently_processed.content: Intelligent systems do not operate in isolation from the body, yet how bodily actions support internal computation remains unclear. Here we show that primates and artificial agents recruit eye movements to maintain beliefs about hidden goals when internal computation is constrained. In a naturalistic navigation task, both systems spontaneously tracked goals with their eyes after they disappeared from view. This strategy emerged in artificial agents only when internal memory was constrained, identifying resource constraints as a driver of memory externalization. Restricting gaze impaired performance in both systems, while natural behavioral variability and causal perturbations in agents established a direct influence of oculomotor state on internal beliefs about hidden goals. Across agents, varying the reliability of internal memory and gaze redistributed goal information between internal and embodied states. The same resource-allocation principle predicted the distribution of goal information in macaque parietal cortex, where greater reliance on gaze was accompanied by weaker gaze-independent neural representations. Together, these findings identify eye movements as embodied memory and reveal a convergent principle across intelligent systems: memory is allocated across internal and embodied resources according to their reliability.
recently_processed.author: Zhang, R., Pitkow, X., Angelaki, D.

recently_processed.title: Dietary vitamin B5 positively regulates intestinal neuropeptide secretion in C. elegans
recently_processed.content: Vitamin B5 is an essential vitamin that must be acquired via diet or by the gut microbiota, and vitamin B5 deficiency or altered vitamin B5 metabolism leads to a variety of physiological and neuronal disorders. We conducted a genetic analysis of the effects of exogenous vitamin B5 in C. elegans, and we found that vitamin B5 confers protection to toxicity caused by oxidative stress and acute exposure to vitamin B5 positively regulates neuropeptide secretion. We identified a sodium-dependent multivitamin transporter family member, smvt-1 that is required for B5 uptake into cells and for protection conferred by vitamin B5. Vitamin B5 positively regulates the intestinal secretion of FLP-2, a neuropeptide-like protein whose release activates the antioxidant response. Vitamin B5 promotes FLP-2 secretion rapidly, specifically, and in a manner that is dependent upon uptake into intestinal cells by smvt-1. Vitamin B5-induced neuropeptide secretion is strictly dependent upon the SNARE protein aex-4/SNAP-25 and on the calcium dependent protein kinase C family member, pkc-2/PKCa in the intestine. These results reveal a previously uncharacterized function for dietary vitamin B5 in positively regulating intestinal neuropeptide secretion from dense core vesicles and in shaping the antioxidant response.
